title: Puro-2B: Pretraining a Real LLM for $6,900
hook: Reproducing SmolLM3-3B costs over $700K. This team pretrained a 2B model on 1.4T tokens using consumer RTX 5090s for under $6.9K — and released the whole recipe.
key_points: Open weights and open training recipes exist, but a cost-efficient, hardware-accessible pretraining recipe was missing.
For scale: the authors cite over $1.5M to train Llama-3.2-3B and over $700K to reproduce SmolLM3-3B.
Puro-2B models are trained from scratch on up to 1.4 trillion tokens in FP8 on consumer-grade RTX 5090 GPUs.
Best model costs under $6.9K of compute and approaches Qwen2.5-1.5B performance under their evaluation protocol.
Enabling ingredients: hardware selection, low-precision training, hyperball optimization, curriculum model averaging, and the data recipe.
A fitted Puro Cost Scaling Law suggests about $4.4K — less than the price of one 5090 at $5,090 — suffices to match Qwen2-1.5B.
content_html: Pretraining a language model has become synonymous with a budget most labs and all hobbyists lack. The authors put numbers on it: over $1.5M to train Llama-3.2-3B, over $700K to reproduce SmolLM3-3B. Open weights and open recipes exist, but an open recipe that is cheap and runs on accessible hardware did not.
extra_html:
What they built

Puro-2B is a collection of models trained from scratch on up to 1.4 trillion tokens, in FP8, on consumer-grade RTX 5090 GPUs. Models in the collection differ in token budget and recipe variant. The best of them costs under $6.9K in compute and approaches Qwen2.5-1.5B performance under the authors' evaluation protocol.

The cost efficiency comes from a stack of choices rather than one trick: hardware selection, low-precision training, hyperball optimization, curriculum model averaging, and the data recipe. All of it — data, code, weights — is released under Apache 2.0.

Two results beyond the recipe

They fit a Puro Cost Scaling Law relating training cost to average performance across the collection; the fit suggests about $4.4K, less than the $5,090 sticker price the GPU is named for, is enough to reach Qwen2-1.5B-level results. And they run an end-to-end case study on how pretraining data curricula shape performance after post-training — the kind of controlled study you can only do when you own the whole pipeline rather than downloading the weights at the end of it.

Why it matters

Frontier-scale pretraining stays out of reach, but the study of pretraining does not have to. A recipe anyone with a few consumer GPUs can rerun turns pretraining from something you read about into something you can experiment on.

related.title: Scaling Laws for Learning Rate and Batch Size
related.hook: Chinchilla told you how many tokens. This tells you what learning rate and batch size to use as you get there — including whether the optimum survives the decay phase.

related.title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
related.hook: Loss doesn't drop randomly as models grow — it follows a smooth power law in size, data, and compute. That predictability is what made betting on bigger models rational.

flashcards.prompt: Why does releasing the full pretraining pipeline enable studies that open weights cannot?
flashcards.back_html: Questions like "how does the data curriculum shape post-training?" require rerunning pretraining under controlled variations. Weights alone fix the curriculum you got.
